title: How the Blue Wave Powered Liberal Judges in Supreme Court Elections
author: Alex Burness
content:
Democrats’ strength in last week’s midterms trickled down to elections for
state supreme courts, powerful bodies that have the final word on all sorts of
major issues—and whose rulings create a patchwork of laws and legal realities
that can vary widely, from abortion access to redistricting.

Twenty-three states were voting on supreme court seats last week, on top of
the eight that already held court elections earlier this year. Some held
retention elections, in which justices faced simple yes-or-no votes to keep
their seats, while others held more conventional, competitive contests.

Democrats or Democratic-backed candidates defended three supreme court seats
in [Michigan](https://boltsmag.org/feed/#MI) and [North
Carolina](https://boltsmag.org/feed/#NC) that Republican challengers hoped to
take over, and flipped five seats across the supreme courts of
[Ohio](https://boltsmag.org/feed/#OH) and
[Texas](https://boltsmag.org/feed/#TX)—adding to their gains on
[Wisconsin](https://boltsmag.org/feed/#WI)’s supreme court in April. In Texas,
Democrats also flipped three seats on the Court of Criminal Appeals, the
state’s high court for criminal cases.

In [Montana](https://boltsmag.org/feed/#MT), the main state where ideological
control was at stake last week, the more liberal candidate prevailed by
roughly 20 percentage points over a GOP-backed candidate. Montana observers
told _Bolts_ that the result solidifies the court’s standing as a
“[backstop](https://boltsmag.org/montana-supreme-court-elections-2024-and-
voting-rights/)” against conservative legislation in the state.

“We had some pause: Is this the election that flips the Supreme Court in the
other direction?” said Keaton Sunchild of the Billings-based Native American
advocacy group Western Native Voice, which has sued the state over
restrictions to ballot access. “When it became apparent it was not, it was a
sigh of relief for our organization and many other organizations around the
state.”

In [Utah](https://boltsmag.org/feed/#UT), a justice survived a retention vote
despite opposition from the GOP, which earlier this year expanded the court by
two seats to make it more conservative. Justices who have drawn Republican
anger in recent years also survived retention in
[Kansas](https://boltsmag.org/feed/#KS),
[Missouri](https://boltsmag.org/feed/#MO), and
[Oklahoma](https://boltsmag.org/feed/#OK).

The GOP’s clearest supreme court successes this year came in elections that
were held this spring in [Arkansas](https://boltsmag.org/feed/#AR) and
[Georgia](https://boltsmag.org/feed/#GA), where GOP-backed justices prevailed.
Republicans may still be able to point at a success in
[Washington](https://boltsmag.org/feed/#WA), where a candidate who drew
support from both Democratic officials and the state Republican Party is
narrowly leading as of publication.

While no court majority outright flipped this year, the results set up intense
competition in the 2028 cycle, largely to Democrats’ benefit.

Democratic gains in Ohio and Texas have put them in the unexpected position to
gain control of these state’s supreme courts in two years. Plus, North
Carolina Justice Anita Earls’ reelection makes for an easier road for
Democrats looking to flip that court in 2028. Meanwhile, Republican losses in
Michigan mean the party can no longer flip that state’s supreme court in two
years, barring an unforeseen retirement.

_Bolts_ walks you through each supreme court race that took place this year,
state by state.

### **Alabama**

Justice Greg Shaw, a Republican, easily defeated AshLeigh Dunham, a Democratic
attorney at a law firm that helps people navigate assisted reproduction like
in vitro fertilization. Dunham said she was [inspired to
run](https://alabamareflector.com/2025/06/05/ashleigh-dunham-announces-
candidacy-for-associate-justice-of-alabama-supreme-court/) by her anger at the
Alabama Supreme Court’s decision in 2024 that held that frozen embryos are
children, which led fertility clinics to [shut
down](https://www.cnn.com/2024/08/14/us/alabama-ivf-clinic-closing); Shaw
voted with the majority in that decision.

Shaw won by 16 percentage points, the narrowest margin for a Republican in a
supreme court election in Alabama since 2018. A second GOP justice, Brad
Mendheim, secured reelection unopposed.

### **Alaska**

Justice Jude Pate easily secured a new term in an up-or-down retention vote,
his first time facing voters since he was appointed to the court by Republican
Governor Mike Dunleavy in 2023.

### **Arizona**

John Lopez IV, a Republican-appointed justice who wrote the court’s [2024
ruling](https://www.azcentral.com/story/news/politics/arizona/2024/04/09/arizona-
abortion-law-state-supreme-court-upholds-near-total-ban/73251148007/) that
outlawed nearly all abortions, easily secured retention with 59 percent of the
vote. That’s roughly the same share of the vote that two of his fellow
conservative justices enjoyed in 2024.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/16354688373650-2400x1727.jpg)Arizona Justice John
Lopez IV is sworn in for his first term in 2016. (AP Photo/Matt York)

No sitting Arizona justice has ever lost an up-or-down retention election. But
the left and the right both tried to shake up the status quo two years ago,
unsuccessfully; progressives mounted an unusually strong effort to convince
voters to oust anti-abortion justices, and conservatives
[asked](https://boltsmag.org/proposition-137-judicial-elections/) Arizonans to
cancel judicial elections altogether. Some change has nevertheless come to the
court since then as Governor Katie Hobbs
[appointed](https://azgovernor.gov/office-arizona-
governor/news/2025/01/governor-katie-hobbs-appoints-judge-maria-elena-cruz-
arizona) Maria Elena Cruz last year, making her the court’s only Democratic-
appointed justice at present.

### **Arkansas**

Justices Nick Bronni and Cody Hiland, two conservative appointees of Governor
Sarah Huckabee Sanders, secured their first full terms in the state’s March
elections. [As _Bolts_ reported at the time](https://boltsmag.org/arkansas-
supreme-court-musical-chairs/), Bronni and Hiland ran for each other’s seats
to get around the state constitution’s prohibition on an appointed justice
running for a full term; they also benefited from a new law that allowed
interim judges to use their new title on the ballot, making it easier for them
to reap the benefits of incumbency. The results fulfilled Huckabee Sanders’
stated goal to “[cement](https://governor.arkansas.gov/news_post/governor-
sanders-appoints-jester-as-secretary-of-state-hiland-and-bronni-to-the-
supreme-court/)” a conservative majority on the court.

But President Donald Trump this week nominated Hiland to a federal judgeship.
If Hiland is confirmed by the U.S. Senate, it would leave yet another state
supreme court vacancy for Huckabee Sanders to fill.

### **California**

Justice Kelli Evans, an appointee of Gavin Newsom, and Justice Joshua Groban,
an appointee of Jerry Brown, easily won their retention elections with over 70
percent of the vote. No California justice has lost retention since
[1986](https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-
xpm-1986-11-05-mn-15232-story.html), though the state's largest police union
[mounted an ad campaign](https://calmatters.org/justice/2026/10/porac-
judicial-election/) this fall to urge voters to oust Evans, saying she was too
amenable to hearing appeals from defendants in criminal cases.

### **Colorado**

Justice William Hood, who joined the court in 2014 after being appointed by
Governor John Hickenlooper, a Democrat, easily won his retention vote with 66
percent of the vote—a margin in line with other recent, uneventful judicial
elections in the state.

### **Florida**

Carlos G. Muñiz secured retention by 15 percentage points, the tightest margin
for a Florida justice in at least a decade, according to data collected on
[Ballotpedia](https://ballotpedia.org/Florida_Supreme_Court_elections,_2026).
No Florida justice has ever lost a retention election, and these contests
typically draw little to no scrutiny, but there was some opposition to Muñiz.
_The Miami Herald_ ’s editorial board
[recommended](https://www.miamiherald.com/opinion/election-
recommendations/article317721420.html) that voters oust him because he was
helping “further a Republican political agenda.”

Muñiz was appointed to the bench by Governor Ron DeSantis in 2022 and he has
since helped make this court a reliable conservative bastion. He voted to
[uphold](https://statecourtreport.org/sites/default/files/2024-04/supreme-
court-of-florida-opinion_sc2022-1050-04.01.2024.pdf) Florida’s six-week
abortion ban in 2024, and this summer he [voted to
uphold](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/florida-supreme-court-
rejects-challenge-new-gop-drawn-congressional-ma-rcna349602) the GOP’s new
congressional gerrymander despite the restrictions on partisan gerrymandering
that [voters placed](https://boltsmag.org/florida-map-fair-districts-
amendments-ruling/) in the state constitution.

### **Georgia**

Republicans lost nearly all levers of power in Georgia last week, letting go
of seven statewide offices, plus the state House and the public service
commission. But a silver lining for the party is that earlier this spring
elections, two GOP-backed justices [prevailed against a pair of liberal
attorneys](https://boltsmag.org/georgia-supreme-court-election-results-2026/).
(There were no judicial seats on the November ballot.)

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/881593661_1394147139166978_4221852459147970524_n.jpeg)Five
of the nine justices on the Georgia supreme court have made it to the bench
via an appointment by outgoing Governor Brian Kemp. Keisha Lance Bottoms, a
Democrat, will replace Kemp. (Facebook/Keisha for Georgia)

The elections, which did not have party identification on the ballot, possibly
blunting the challengers given the political environment, revolved largely
around voting rights and abortion.

Georgia’s judicial elections this decade have been marred by [a
loophole](https://boltsmag.org/dystopian-loophole-for-judicial-elections-
gives-brian-kemp-the-last-laugh/) in state law that allows public officials to
cancel elections even when candidates are already running—[potentially even
after the election](https://boltsmag.org/georgia-judicial-elections-loophole-
scrutiny/) has been held. The loophole has been wielded by Republican Governor
Brian Kemp, though the power to appoint judges will now be in the hands of
Keisha Lance Bottoms, the first Democrat to win a governor’s race since 1998.

Sara Tindall Ghazal, a Democratic [member](https://www.theguardian.com/us-
news/article/2024/aug/13/sara-tindall-ghazal-georgia-state-election-board) of
the Georgia Board of Elections who told _Bolts_ [last
year](https://boltsmag.org/georgia-judicial-elections-loophole-scrutiny/) that
lawmakers should close the loophole, said this week that she still wants to
see that reform. She also called on lawmakers to consider another change:
moving the timing of judicial elections from the spring to the higher-turnout
November elections “so that more voters weigh in on these important seats.”

### **Idaho**

There was zero suspense in Idaho: No one challenged Justices Cynthia Meyer and
Gregory Moeller, so they both won a new term unopposed. All Idaho supreme
court races have been uncontested since 2018.

### **Kansas**

A landmark decision by the Kansas Supreme Court in 2019 protected abortion
access in the state. It also intensified conservative efforts to change the
direction of the court. But their aspirations suffered a series of major
setbacks this year.

First, Kansans in August [rejected a GOP-sponsored ballot
measure](https://boltsmag.org/kansas-supreme-court-ballot-measure-defeat-and-
new-judicial-appointments/) that would have changed how justices are selected
for the court and likely pushed it to the right; that referendum was seen as a
proxy for the debate over abortion rights.

Then, Kansans voted last week to retain Justices Eric Rosen and Larkin Walsh.
Rosen has been on the court since 2005 and he joined the majority in upholding
abortion access in 2019. He beat back an [intense
effort](https://www.kcur.org/politics-elections-and-
government/2014-11-04/kansas-judges-targeted-for-ouster-retain-seats) to oust
him over his votes to overturn two death sentences in 2014, but conservatives
did not mount such an organized campaign this year.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/729754649_1041998748766156_5908738494564126883_n.jpg)Kansas
Justice Larkin Walsh was appointed by Governor Laura Kelly in 2025 and she was
retained by voters in this election. (Facebook/Kansas Judicial Branch)

Walsh, meanwhile, is a recent appointee of Governor Laura Kelly, a Democrat.
She has yet to participate in many major decisions, but her vote to strike
down restrictions on mail voting this summer hinted that a new majority more
amenable to voting rights cases may be emerging, [as _Bolts_ previously
reported](https://boltsmag.org/kansas-supreme-court-ballot-measure-defeat-and-
new-judicial-appointments/).

Earlier this decade, the Kansas Supreme Court sided with Republicans in two
4-3 decisions that upheld a GOP gerrymander and rejected protections for a
fundamental right to vote. Rosen dissented from both rulings. “It staggers my
imagination to conclude Kansas citizens have no fundamental right to vote
under their state constitution,” he wrote, and it’s possible that Rosen now
has enough allies to find himself in the majority on this issue should the
court revisit it.

### **Kentucky**  

Debra Hembree Lambert, a conservative justice who represents the state’s
deeply-Republican third judicial district, secured a new term without facing
any opponent.

### **Louisiana**

Two justices, Republicans Cade Cole and Jay McCallum, ran for reelection
entirely unopposed this year. In a third contest in Louisiana’s first judicial
district, which covers the staunchly conservative St. Tammany Parish, voters
this year chose a replacement to William Crain, who was nominated to the
federal bench by Trump last year. William Burris won the GOP’s primary for
that open seat in May [with
support](https://lailluminator.com/2026/02/02/burris-supreme-court/) from
conservative business groups, and he did not face an opponent in last week’s
general election.

### **Maryland  **

Justice Peter Killough, who was appointed to the court by Democratic Governor
Wes Moore in 2024,
[triumphed](https://elections.maryland.gov/elections/2026/general_results/gen_results_2026_8.html)
in his first retention election with roughly 86 percent of the vote. The
state’s retention elections tend to produce particularly large margins for
incumbents even by national standards.

### **Michigan**

Democrats defended their towering 6-1 majority on this court. Despite
Michigan’s reputation as a swing state, Democratic incumbents Megan Cavanagh
and Noah Hood easily prevailed over Michael Warren and Casandra Morse-Bills,
two Republican lower court judges.  

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/886684666_18347755372249231_4679696242718748158_n-
edited-2400x1784.jpg)Democratic incumbents justices Noah Hood (left) and Megan
Cavanagh easily prevailed over two Republican lower court judges in Tuesday's
election. (Facebook/Megan Cavanagh)

The results mean that Republicans cannot flip the court until at least 2030,
barring an unforeseen retirement. They needed to flip at least one of the two
seats on this fall’s ballot to have a shot at gaining the majority in two
years, when two more Democratic justices, Kyra Harris Bolden and Elizabeth
Welch, are up for reelection.

The Michigan Supreme Court has in recent years chipped away at punitive
criminal statutes, including in a series of major decisions that [have
restricted](https://boltsmag.org/michigan-supreme-court-young-adults-life-
sentences/) sentences of life without parole for young adults. Hood, who only
joined the court in the spring of 2025, voted with Cavanagh and other
Democrats in such a case for [the first time this
summer](https://www.michiganpublic.org/criminal-justice-legal-
system/2026-07-28/michigan-supreme-court-again-limits-life-without-parole-
this-time-in-narrow-ruling). The court also
[decided](https://www.wilx.com/2026/09/12/michigan-supreme-court-rules-state-
cannot-enforce-sex-offender-registry-law-against-some-longtime-registrants/)
unanimously this fall that thousands of people had to be removed from the
state’s sex offender registry because they were being subjected to rules that
did not exist at the time of their conviction.

### **Minnesota**

Two justices, Sarah Hennesy and Paul Thissen, faced no challengers in November
and so coasted to reelection. Hennesy and Thissen were both appointed by
Democratic governors, but they have a second—and more unusual—trait in common;
they’re both former public defenders. Progressives nationwide have [pushed
for](https://boltsmag.org/public-defenders-state-supreme-courts/) more public
defenders on state courts, and while they often fall short, there are
currently three former public defenders on [Minnesota’s bench](https://state-
law-research.org/states/minnesota/).

### **Missouri**

When the Missouri Supreme Court unanimously voted to block a Republican
congressional gerrymander in September and threatened to hold the secretary of
state in contempt for nevertheless trying to use the map, some conservatives
vowed [revenge](https://www.kshb.com/news/local-news/republicans-threaten-
impeachment-of-missouri-supreme-court-if-hoskins-found-in-contempt). But Paul
Wilson, the only justice on the ballot this fall, [easily
prevailed](https://boltsmag.org/missourians-veto-new-gerrymander-and-make-it-
trickier-for-gop-to-adopt-another/) in an up-or-down retention vote with
roughly 63 percent of the vote.

Wilson, a 2012 appointee of Democratic Governor Jay Nixon, has bucked
Republican state officials in other cases—for instance, he wrote a 2024 ruling
that [struck down](https://apnews.com/article/ballot-amendment-new-vote-
missouri-kansas-city-police-funding-2ce4cbd5c1f6f991946bfc66f5dac143) a
constitutional amendment requiring Kansas City to spend more money on police.
Last year, he was one of two dissenting justices when the [court
denied](https://molawyersmedia.com/2025/06/17/missouri-transgender-student-
discrimination-case/) a transgender student’s claims of discrimination.

### **Montana**

Montana hosted the only race this year that could have outright flipped the
ideological majority on any state’s supreme court. But no such shift occurred,
as Amy Eddy, a Flathead County judge who was backed by a slew of liberal
groups, [trounced](https://montanafreepress.org/2026/11/03/amy-eddy-wins-
montana-supreme-court-election/) Dan Wilson, another Flathead County judge,
who touted his “conservative judicial philosophy.”

Eddy’s win means that the seven-member nonpartisan court will continue to
feature four justices who have won with liberal backing. The court [has been a
thorn](https://boltsmag.org/montana-supreme-court-elections-2024-and-voting-
rights/) in the side of Republicans in Montana, striking down limits on voter
access, abortion, and transgender rights.

She will replace outgoing Justice Beth Baker, who herself was elected with
liberal backing and has voted against conservative reforms in major cases,
though she has at times been a swing vote on the court.

Keaton Sunchild, a voting rights advocate who leads government relations work
for the group Western Native Voice, called Eddy’s win a “relief.” Western
Native Voice led a coalition of tribes that sued after the state legislature
made various elections changes, including [ending](https://apnews.com/general-
news-5ee83eb24b3339610cfaee3570a16e4f) same-day voter registration; the state
supreme court in 2024 [sided with this
coalition](https://montanafreepress.org/2024/03/27/montana-supreme-court-
declares-2021-voting-laws-unconstitutional/), preventing the Republican
reforms from going into effect.

“We never want to have to rest on the fact that something will get sorted out
in the courts. It’s still our very last resort,” he said. “But it is
reassuring to know that a lot of the work we’re doing and will continue to do
has been upheld multiple times with this court.”

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/706744810_122239548488057860_4795009944533581667_n-
edited-e1794418650799.jpg)Amy Eddy, a Flathead County judge, sailed to victory
in Montana's supreme court election over a judge who touted his “conservative
judicial philosophy.” (Amy Eddy campaign/Facebook)

Also on the ballot Tuesday in Montana was a proposed
[amendment](https://dailymontanan.com/2026/11/04/montanans-overwhelmingly-
approve-3-ballot-measures/) codifying in the state constitution that judicial
elections remain nonpartisan, which passed with more than two-thirds support
from voters. The amendment, which can now only be reversed through another
popular vote, thwarts any future actions from GOP lawmakers to make court
elections partisan.

### **Nevada**  

A blue tsunami swept Democrats into all the statewide offices for which they
ran, and also delivered them the county commission in Washoe County, home to
Reno, [for the first time
ever](https://thenevadaindependent.com/article/northern-nevada-results-dems-
take-historic-control-of-washoe-commission-sweep-reno-races). But there’ll be
no change on the Nevada Supreme Court as two conservative justices, Doug
Herndon and Kris Pickering, were facing no challengers and coasted to
reelection unbothered.

### **New Mexico**

Two justices, Shannon Bacon and David Thompson, easily secured retention, a
result that keeps this all-Democratic court intact.

### **North Carolina**

Justice Anita Earls, a Democrat and former voting rights attorney, easily
prevailed last week over Sarah Stevens, a longtime Republican lawmaker. She
won 59 to 41 percent, a startling margin given Republican hopes in this
contest that mirrors the broader blue tsunami in the state.

As __[_Bolts_ reported in September](https://boltsmag.org/north-carolina-
supreme-court-election-2026/), the future of voting rights loomed large over
the race. Earls is a former voting rights attorney who has voted to strike
down GOP gerrymanders and voter restrictions, while Stevens has championed
many of those Republican election laws.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Earls.jpg)North Carolina
Justice Anita Earls in Saxapahaw, North Carolina, in 2025 (photo from
Earls/Facebook)

Earls told _Bolts_ that she encountered voters that were worried about whether
democracy in North Carolina is “going to work the way we believe it should in
America.” She said that when she first ran for a seat on the court in 2018,
“There wasn’t the same fear that our democratic processes have been hijacked
and interrupted.”

Earls’ win doesn’t change the GOP’s comfortable, 5-2 majority on the court.
But it does preserve Democrats’ path to flipping the court’s majority in 2028,
when three Republican-held seats will be on the ballot; Democrats would need
to win two of those three seats. The last time the court flipped after the
2022 midterms, the new GOP majority quickly overturned recent election law
cases—including blessing a Republican gerrymander that it had just struck
down.

### **North Dakota**

Justice Jerod Tufte secured reelection over Ariston Johnson, a local attorney,
by a wide margin, 65 to 35 percent. Tufte
[voted](https://northdakotamonitor.com/2025/11/21/breaking-north-dakota-
abortion-ban-deemed-constitutional-in-split-opinion-from-state-supreme-court/)
to uphold the state’s abortion ban last year in a case that would have gone
the other way had Tufte voted differently; Johnson, who [leaned
heavily](https://northdakotamonitor.com/2026/09/21/north-dakota-supreme-court-
races-are-nonpartisan-but-republicans-play-a-big-role/) on a promise to be
nonpartisan and not court party endorsements, but who still signaled his
alignment with conservative jurists, does not appear to have made the abortion
case into a campaign issue.

A second justice, Douglas Bahr, was unopposed and coasted to securing his
first full term.

### **Ohio**

While Democrats had been on the verge of disappearing from the Ohio Supreme
Court heading into the midterms, a strong night for their party allowed them
to keep one seat and flip another.

Justice Jennifer Brunner, currently the lone Democrat on the court, has been
left writing lonely dissents in high-profile decisions, [such as a case last
year](https://signalcleveland.org/ohio-supreme-court-rules-nitrogen-gas-that-
suffocated-a-timkensteel-worker-was-non-toxic/) that held that the family of a
security guard who suffocated from nitrogen gas at his workplace could not sue
for damages. Just last month, Brunner [was the only justice to
say](https://www.nbc4i.com/news/local-news/columbus/ohio-court-refusing-
police-for-mental-health-commitment-can-result-in-obstruction-charge/) that a
woman who resisted an involuntary mental health commitment cannot be charged
with obstructing police business. The ruling “turns having a mental illness
into a crime,” Brunner wrote.

Brunner secured a third term last week over Republican Colleen O’Donnell, a
former local judge in Franklin County; she won by three percentage points. And
she will be joined on the bench by fellow Democrat Marilyn Zayas, a lower
court judge who ousted Republican Justice Daniel Hawkins __by two points.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/26126783895737-2400x1601.jpg)Justice Jennifer Brunner
speaks at a primary election night campaign event in her bid for re-election
on Tuesday, May 5 in Columbus, Ohio. (AP Photo/Jay LaPrete)

Republicans still retain a comfortable 5-2 majority, but the results mean that
Democrats have a shot at flipping the court in two years, when multiple GOP-
held seats [will be on the
ballot](https://ballotpedia.org/State_supreme_court_elections,_2028), and one
Republican incumbent [is barred from seeking
reelection](https://signalohio.org/fischer-drops-out-of-2026-ohio-supreme-
court-election/) due to his age.

### **Oklahoma**

Conservatives in 2024 [managed to defeat](https://boltsmag.org/state-supreme-
court-results-2024/) a sitting justice in a retention vote for the first time
in Oklahoma’s history. They were upset by decisions made by Yvonne Kauger, who
voted with the court’s majority in 2023 to uphold a narrow right for women to
access abortion if their life is in danger; two other justices who joined
Kauger in that decision narrowly survived.

This year, some conservatives
[targeted](https://www.oklahomastatecapital.com/news/article/2026/10/21/OPINION%3A%2BThe%2BNovember%2BBallot%2BNo%2BOne%2BIs%2BTalking%2BAbout%3A%2BWhich%2BOklahoma%2BJudges%2BShould%2BStay%E2%80%94and%2BWhich%2BShould%2BGo/329482cd-b41f-4418-85b5-c1bc334590f4)
Justice Richard Darby, an appointee of former Republican Governor Mary Fallin.
Darby dissented in the 2023 abortion case but he
[angered](https://ocpathink.org/post/analysis/oklahoma-supreme-court-weakens-
election-integrity-legislature-forced-to-fix-it) the right in 2020 when he
sided with the majority in a decision that removed some restrictions on mail
voting during the COVID-19 pandemic. The conservative group Oklahoma Council
of Public Affairs (OCPA), which aired ads to oust Kauger and her two
colleagues in 2024, did not mobilize against Darby in the same way this year,
[according to the _Oklahoma City
Journal_](https://oklahomacityrecord.com/articles/four-oklahoma-supreme-court-
justices-face-nov-3-retention-vote-mva5yqfs), but it released a judicial
[scorecard](https://ocpathink.org/judicial-scorecard) to showcase that they
were not satisfied with him.

Darby prevailed 53 to 47 percent last week, a narrow margin by the usual
standards of retention contests, while the other three justices on the ballot
with a much more favorable score from the OCPA—Travis Jett, John Kane, and
Dana Kuehn—prevailed with 57 or 58 percent of the vote. Rob Hudson, a judge on
the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals, the state’s high court for criminal
matters, also secured reelection with 57 percent of the vote.

On Tuesday, one week after he survived retention, Darby joined a 5-4
[ruling](https://bsky.app/profile/redistrictnet.xpost.bot/post/3mzye45v2sz2j)
that struck down a law passed by state Republicans last year to restrict
ballot initiatives.

Conservatives have also tried to affect Oklahoma courts by changing how judges
make it on the bench in the first place. Currently, [to fill a
vacancy](https://boltsmag.org/whats-on-the-ballot/state-supreme-courts/#OK),
an independent commission forwards a short list to the governor; the person
selected by the governor later faces a retention vote. Republicans placed a
measure on November’s ballot that would have given them more control over the
nominating commission, but voters overwhelmingly
[rejected](https://oklahomavoice.com/2026/11/03/voters-give-thumbs-down-to-
oklahoma-legislatures-attempt-to-reform-judiciary-selections/) it.

### **Oregon**

Justice Chris Garrett, who joined the court in 2019 after being appointed by
former Democratic Governor Kate Brown, did not face any opponent and coasted
to a second term.

### **Tennessee**

Two justices easily retained their seats in up-or-down votes, securing more
than 70 percent of the vote, in elections that were held in August rather than
in November. Justice Mary Wagner, who used to work for the Tennessee
Republican Party, joined the court in 2024 via Republican Governor Bill Lee’s
nomination. Justice Kyle Hixson, who highlighted his alignment with
conservative jurists [during his selection
process](https://nashvillebanner.com/2026/01/23/kyle-hixson-tennessee-supreme-
court-gov-bill-lee-nominee/), was named to the court earlier this year.

### **Texas**

Democrats had not won any statewide election in Texas in 32 years. That streak
ended in spectacular fashion on Tuesday when the party swept all statewide
races on the ballot and flipped seven seats across the state’s two high
courts.

Democrats ousted four incumbent Republicans from the Texas Supreme Court,
which has final say in civil cases, narrowing the GOP majority to 5-4.

They also flipped three GOP-held seats on the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals,
which has the final say on criminal cases, narrowing the GOP majority to 6-3.

Maggie Ellis’s victory over Chief Justice Jimmy Blacklock makes her the first
LGBTQ+ candidate to win any statewide election in Texas, [according to
KXAN](https://www.kxan.com/news/your-local-election-hq/texas-1st-lgbtq-
elected-to-statewide-office-in-texas/). She [said last
week](https://www.click2houston.com/news/local/2026/11/06/texas-chief-justice-
elect-seeks-to-end-religious-exemptions-for-judges-officiating-weddings/) that
she wants to end a rule [recently put in
place](https://www.texastribune.org/2025/10/29/texas-judges-gay-marriages-
rule-supreme-court/) by the Texas Supreme Court that allows local judges to
decline to officiate same-sex weddings when they say it conflicts with their
religious beliefs.

Ellis will be joined on the supreme court by fellow Democrats Chari Kelly,
Kristen Hawkins, and Gisela Triana. The new Democratic judges on the court of
criminal appeals are Okey Anyiam, Audra Riley, and Holly Taylor.

Democrats are now in a position to flip both of Texas’ high courts in 2028,
when the GOP must defend three seats on each.

But the results could also affect cases before then if the incoming Democrats
band together and coalesce with one or two of the Republican judges who remain
on the court, injecting some new uncertainty into legal proceedings that
conservatives have gotten used to dominating.

The Texas Supreme Court often [issued unanimous
decisions](https://mail.google.com/), such as when it [upheld the state's
strict ban on abortion](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c8881d31j44o)—but
dissenting voices have also emerged in other major cases.

For instance, when the court [upheld a GOP
law](https://www.texastribune.org/2024/06/28/texas-supreme-court-gender-
affirming-care-2/) that restricted gender-affirming care for minors in 2024,
the vote was 8 to 1, with a lone dissent from Justice Debra Lehrmann. Lehrmann
also dissented from a ruling that [tossed
out](https://www.texastribune.org/2024/12/31/texas-attorney-general-state-bar-
lawsuit-dismissed-brent-webster/) the Texas State Bar’s effort to discipline a
top attorney working under Attorney General Ken Paxton for trying to overturn
the 2020 presidential election.

Lehrmann’s seat was not up this fall, so she’s now set to sit alongside the
four Democrats.

The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals has similar divides. In September, when
the court [issued](https://www.texastribune.org/2026/09/24/texas-death-row-
melissa-lucio-appeal-denied/) [a deeply
divided](https://deathpenaltyinfo.org/texas-court-of-criminal-appeals-refuses-
to-grant-relief-to-melissa-lucio-despite-trial-courts-finding-of-actual-
innocence) ruling that rejected a lower court’s finding that death row
prisoner Melissa Lucio was innocent, four of nine judges dissented. Only one
of them is leaving the court (David Newell, who did not seek reelection); Lee
Finley, David Schenck, and Scott Walker remain.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/22118021357214-2400x1600.jpg)Supporters hold signs up
as they chant "Free Melissa Lucio" in April of 2022 in Cameron County, Texas.
(Denise Cathey/The Brownsville Herald via AP)

In fact, Kevin Yeary, a judge who was just ousted from this court last week,
has a history of consistently opposing fully exonerating prisoners. [_Texas
Monthly_ reports](https://www.texasmonthly.com/news-politics/court-of-
criminal-appeals-election-democrats/) that he insisted on an exacting legal
standards that few cases can meet, and frequently pushed back against
colleagues who wanted to recognize someone’s actual innocence. His departure
could affect how the court approaches wrongful conviction cases, as could the
election of Holly Taylor, a Democrat who worked in the wrongful conviction
unit of the Travis County DA’s office.

### **Utah**

It ended up being a sleepy Election Day on the supreme court front in Utah:
Jill Pohlman, a justice who has drawn attacks from state Republicans for
joining rulings [limiting](https://boltsmag.org/utah-supreme-court-direct-
democracy/) the legislature’s power to gerrymander and
[preventing](https://www.aclu.org/wp-content/plugins/pdfjs-viewer-
shortcode/pdfjs/web/viewer.php) a near-total abortion ban from taking effect,
[easily won her retention
election](https://utahnewsdispatch.com/2026/11/03/utah-supreme-court-justice-
jill-pohlman-retention-vote/).

The Utah GOP had
[signaled](https://www.sltrib.com/news/politics/2026/04/28/utah-republican-
leaders-urge/) it would try to defeat her retention but court watchers say no
significant campaign materialized; she was retained with about 77 percent of
the vote, just three percentage points off the [average retention
margin](https://ballotpedia.org/State_supreme_court_retention_election_results,_1990-present)
for Utah justices since 1990.

But Pohlman’s victory is only a minor story for a court that has otherwise
changed enormously this year, thanks largely to a GOP power grab. Frustrated
with the state supreme court’s 2025
[rejection](https://www.deseret.com/utah/2025/09/16/utah-supreme-court-
rejects-legislatures-request-to-stop-redistricting/) of their gerrymandering
attempt—among other rulings—Utah’s Republican legislature and governor teamed
up in January to expand the court from five seats to seven.

They also launched an investigation into Justice Diana Hagen, whom they
accused of an “inappropriate” relationship with an attorney in the
gerrymandering case, which prompted her to
[resign](https://www.sltrib.com/news/politics/2026/05/08/supreme-court-
justice-diana-hagen/) in May. Critics of the legislature accused GOP officials
of harassing Hagen out of her job.

The court expansion, plus Hagen’s resignation and the retirement in late
August of Chief Justice Matthew Durrant, handed Governor Spencer Cox power to
fill four seats with conservative jurists—enough for a new ideological
majority on the now-seven-member court.

“I think part of the reason Republicans didn’t come harder against Jill
Pohlman is because they didn’t need her anymore,” Teneille Brown, a University
of Utah law professor and board president of the nonpartisan group Co-Equal
Utah, told _Bolts_. “They’d done the math, and they’ll be able to vote as a
bloc in a way that runs counter to our civil liberties, to democracy.”

The court’s GOP makeover, Brown and others note, could very well push future
gerrymandering and abortion cases over the line.

“Do I have faith in the Supreme Court? No, I don’t,” Brown said, adding, of
Cox’s appointees, “They are the fruits of the poisonous tree. They come from a
process that is now political. It’s all about the outcome, and [Republicans]
got what they wanted. They played the long game and it’s hurt the legitimacy
of our courts.”

### **Washington**

Washington’s was the only supreme court in the nation where most seats were on
the ballot at once—five out of nine. Voters there rejected the potential for
major upheaval by reelecting the three incumbents on the ballot—Colleen
Melody, Theo Angelis, and Debra Stephens. Each had been nominated by a
Democratic governor, and each faced a conservative opponent recommended by the
state Republican Party.

Voters were also filling two open seats. For the Position 3 contest to replace
Justice Racquel Montoya-Lewis, one of the court’s more [left-
leaning](https://boltsmag.org/state-courts-advance-civil-rights/) members,
voters elected Jaime Michelle Hawk, a former ACLU advocate who now serves as a
lower-court judge. Hawk prevailed over a conservative attorney who was
recommended by the state GOP—another win for continuity.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/586525842_1426271612187720_4015826313335030351_n.jpg)Governor
Bob Ferguson (right) appointed Colleen Melody to the Washington supreme court
in 2025, and Melody prevailed over a challenger this month. (Facebook/Governor
Bob Ferguson)

The final seat on the court remains too close to call. To replace Charles
Johnson, a justice who has been on the court since 1991, voters chose between
two lower-court judges, Ian Birk and Sean O’Donnell.

Birk and O’Donnell each drew endorsements from Democratic officials when they
joined the race—Birk, for instance, had the support of former Governor Jay
Inslee, and O’Donnell that of former Governor Christine Gregoire. But the
state Republican Party’s decision to [recommend a
vote](https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2026/sep/15/trial-judge-appellate-
judge-battle-for-open-washin/) for O’Donnell this fall seems to have polarized
the election along partisan lines. O’Donnell [received heavy
support](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/11/03/us/elections/results-
washington-supreme-court-position-4.html) in conservative counties last week
and leads by two percentage points as of publication, with hundreds of
thousands of ballots left to count.

### **West Virginia**

This was a rare state in which voters ousted incumbents in supreme court races
this year: Two justices who’d been appointed by Republican Governor Patrick
Morrisey [lost their bids for full
terms](https://westvirginiawatch.com/2026/05/12/flanigan-wins-west-virginia-
supreme-court-seat-over-morrisey-appointee-ewing/) on this court in
nonpartisan May contests.

One of them, Gerald Titus, lost in a competitive, five-way race won by H.L.
Kirkpatrick, who was previously a local judge for 30 years in West Virginia’s
Raleigh County.

The other incumbent, Tom Ewing, lost in a blowout to longtime Republican state
lawmaker Bill Flanigan, who has stood out for criticizing his own party’s
attacks on LGBTQ+ people, including by [speaking
out](https://mountainstatespotlight.org/2025/04/13/wv-legislative-session-
wrapup/) about suicide among trans youth. Flanigan told _Bolts_ earlier this
year that he was moved when he joined neighbors in helping with recovery work
after a [deadly flood](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/06/26/us/politics/west-
virginia-flood-death-toll.html) hit northern West Virginia.

“For the four weeks we were all doing this, nobody asked what someone’s
sexuality was, or anything other than, ‘What do you need?’” he said. “We don’t
care about that stuff. We want to be free and be left alone. We hear a lot of
the far-left and far-right on the issues, but I think a lot of the state wants
to see us do good work and represent them getting better jobs, having roads
fixed, having clean water.”

### **Wisconsin**

Liberals [extended their majority](https://boltsmag.org/wisconsin-supreme-
court-election-2026-taylor-wins/) on the Wisconsin Supreme Court to 5-2 last
April, when Chris Taylor, an appeals court judge, easily prevailed in the
contest to replace the retiring conservative Rebecca Bradley. Wisconsin has
seen a series of [extraordinarily expensive](https://boltsmag.org/wisconsin-
supreme-court-result-2025/) and contentious supreme court elections, but the
actual results in the state’s last four contests, dating back to 2020, have
not even been close. Taylor won by 20 percentage points last week.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Taylor.png)Chris Taylor,
here shown during her campaign, won the supreme court election in Wisconsin in
April. (Photo via Taylor’s campaign/Facebook)

The result locked in liberal control through at least 2030. In fact, liberals
have an opportunity to cushion their majority further in Wisconsin’s next
judicial elections, which are next April. Justice Annette Ziegler, another
conservative, is not seeking reelection. Both candidates who have so far
announced lean liberal.

### **Wyoming**

There was no backlash at the ballot box to the Wyoming Supreme Court’s
landmark decision in January to strike down the state’s abortion ban. Voters
retained both Justice Robert Jarosh, whose vote against the abortion ban was
decisive, and Justice Bridget Hill, a newcomer who didn’t take part in that
decision but who had defended the ban in court as attorney general. They both
received above 75 percent of the vote.

### **Honorable mention: Mississippi**

This state was supposed to elect supreme court justices this year under fairer
districts after a federal court struck down the current map as unfair to Black
voters.

But the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in April to gut the Voting Rights Act
effectively erased Black plaintiffs’ legal win and canceled the prospect of
elections for the state supreme court, [_Bolts_ and _The Marshall Project_
reported](https://boltsmag.org/callais-ruling-and-mississippi-supreme-court/).
Democrats fared well in other elections that took place in Mississippi last
week, with a surge in Black turnout powering the party to a possible win in
the U.S. Senate race.
